title: SQL RIGHT JOIN
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and row-preservation behaviour of SQL RIGHT JOIN.
Write valid SQLite queries using the join and an explicit ON condition.
Predict the effect of matching, unmatched and one-to-many rows.
Interpret NULL-extended columns and distinguish unmatched rows from matched values.
Recognize SQL dialect and database-version compatibility considerations.

understand.concept: RIGHT JOIN preserves every row from the right input and attaches matching rows from the left input. When no left-side row matches, left-side columns become NULL. The OUTER keyword is optional in RIGHT OUTER JOIN.
understand.whyItMatters: It can be useful when the right-hand table defines the complete population that a report must retain. Reversing table order and using LEFT JOIN is often clearer and more portable.
understand.analogy: It is like keeping every entry in the second list and looking up corresponding entries in the first.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not express SQL NULL behaviour, row multiplication, or whether a particular engine version implements RIGHT JOIN.

examples.title: Create and inspect the sample data
examples.explanation: The right input will be orders, so all four order rows must appear in a RIGHT JOIN result.

examples.title: Preserve every order
examples.expectedOutput: 101 | Asha Rao; 102 | Asha Rao; 103 | Chitra Das; 104 | NULL
examples.explanation: Order 104 is retained even though customer_id 9 has no matching customer.

examples.title: Identify orders without a customer match
examples.explanation: A NULL value in the non-nullable customer primary key indicates that no customer row matched.

examples.title: Express the same preservation with LEFT JOIN
examples.expectedOutput: 101 | Asha Rao; 102 | Asha Rao; 103 | Chitra Das; 104 | NULL
examples.explanation: Swapping the table order and using LEFT JOIN preserves the same order population and is supported by older SQLite versions.

examples.title: Filter the right-side population without dropping unmatched orders
examples.expectedOutput: 101 | Asha Rao; 102 | Asha Rao; 103 | NULL; 104 | NULL
examples.explanation: The ON condition defines qualifying matches while the RIGHT JOIN still preserves every order.

practise.guidedTask: Run the shared setup and execute each SQL RIGHT JOIN example. Before each query, mark which customer and order rows you expect to remain; then compare your prediction with the actual result.
practise.independentTask: Create departments and employees tables with at least five departments and six employees. Include at least one department with no employees and one employee with no department. Write five queries using the join type from this lesson, including one aggregate and one unmatched-row report.
hints: Start by identifying which table must be preserved.
Write the ON predicate using the actual relationship keys.
Add ORDER BY for deterministic output.
Use a non-nullable primary key to detect a missing match.
Check the DBMS version before relying on RIGHT or FULL OUTER JOIN.

options: Every row from the right input
Every row from the left input only
Every row from the right input only
questions.answer: Every row from the right input
questions.explanation: The selected join type determines which unmatched rows remain.

questions.prompt: Where is the relationship between the input rows normally specified?
questions.explanation: ON contains the join predicate that determines matching pairs.

questions.prompt: What can happen when one row matches two rows on the other side?
options: The row can appear twice in the result
The join changes to CROSS JOIN
questions.answer: The row can appear twice in the result
questions.explanation: A join returns matching row pairs, so one-to-many relationships multiply output rows.

questions.prompt: What is a safe way to avoid ambiguous column references?
options: Qualify columns with table names or aliases
Rename every column after the query
questions.answer: Qualify columns with table names or aliases
questions.explanation: Qualified names identify which input supplies a column.

questions.prompt: What should be checked when using this join across database engines?
questions.explanation: Join support and syntax details can vary by engine and version.
